title: How Mitsubishi Pencil Beat the Giant & Bought LAMY
description:
Stamped with three red diamonds, Mitsubishi Pencil states right on its website: "We have no affiliation with the Mitsubishi Group." How did this independent pen maker register the Mitsubishi trademark over a decade before the giant conglomerate—and acquire German fountain pen icon LAMY in 2024?
For anyone who grew up assuming Mitsubishi Pencil was a conglomerate side hustle, or ever wondered about the story behind uni and JETSTREAM.

Drawing on Mitsubishi Pencil Co., Ltd. (7976) official history and FAQ, FY2025 consolidated financial results, the 2024 announcement of the 100% acquisition of C. Josef Lamy GmbH, 2025–2026 press releases for LAMY safari JETSTREAM inside, LAMY safari KURUTOGA inside, and its color-only trademark, plus Mitsubishi Group's official history and trademark management records (mitsubishi.com), this video traces the full story: the 1887 waterwheel workshop in Naito-Shinjuku, the 1901 Ministry of Communications order and 1903 Trademark Registration No. 18865 filed 11 years ahead of the conglomerate, the 1958 wine-red uni and 2018 color trademark, the 100-million-a-year JETSTREAM and 17-year #1 KURUTOGA patent moats, and how buying 1930-founded LAMY pushed overseas revenue past 57% as the company targets ¥94 billion for its 140th anniversary in 2026.

This channel has no affiliation with any brands mentioned. Illustrations in this episode are AI-generated.
Data as of 2026-11-22

m001.text: Look at that wine-red pencil or ultra-smooth pen on your desk.

m002.text: With three red diamonds, 90% assume it's a conglomerate pen.

m003.text: A giant making cars, ships, and banks—why not pens too?

m004.text: Yet Mitsubishi Pencil's site says: no ties to Mitsubishi Group!

m005.text: Wait—an even bigger twist is coming.

m006.text: The pen maker registered the Mitsubishi mark over ten years earlier!

m007.text: In 2024, it even bought German fountain pen icon LAMY!

m008.text: How did an independent pen maker pull all this off?

m009.text: Our researchers dug into Meiji trademark ledgers and financial filings.

m010.text: Today, let's unpack this century-old name clash and comeback!

m011.text: In 1870, Mitsubishi founder Yataro Iwasaki launched a shipping firm,

m012.text: painting three diamonds on ship flags—starting Japan's famed zaibatsu.

m013.text: It fused his former lord's leaf crest with his family's stacked diamonds.

m014.text: Three years later it became Mitsubishi Shokai, sweeping into finance!

m015.text: The giant was already famous—so how did a pencil shop file first?

m016.text: Niroku Masaki, future founder of Mitsubishi Pencil, visited Paris in 1878.

m017.text: At the World's Fair, he saw Western pencils and vowed to make them.

m018.text: Japan imported every single one—no machines, no formulas, pure trial!

m019.text: After nine tough years, he built a Shinjuku waterwheel mill in 1887.

m020.text: He founded Masaki Manufacturing—but did the little mill take off?

m021.text: It nearly failed: leads snapped easily, and wood split when sharpened!

m022.text: He refined lead and wood for 14 years until quality matched imports.

m023.text: In 1901 came the break: Japan's postal ministry adopted his pencils!

m024.text: It ordered three hardness grades for official government use.

m025.text: Japan's first domestic government pencil order—he wanted a proud mark.

m026.text: That quick commemorative sketch sparked a century-long coincidence!

m027.text: Never thinking of the zaibatsu, he drew on his family's three-scale crest.

m028.text: He stretched three scales into three diamonds for the grades—Mitsubishi!

m029.text: In 1903, he formally filed Trademark Registration No. 18865.

m030.text: The giant used it unregistered until 1914—eleven years later!

m031.text: Wait: the Mitsubishi Group guards its mark fiercely. Why no lawsuit?

m032.text: Today its trademark committee controls over 4,500 trademarks!

m033.text: Spanning 140 countries, its site warns copycats of legal action.

m034.text: Yet for over a century, it couldn't touch this pencil company!

m035.text: First, the pen maker legally registered first, holding prior rights.

m036.text: Second, it stuck strictly to stationery—zero clash with heavy industry.

m037.text: In 1952, Masaki unified name and mark as Mitsubishi Pencil.

m038.text: Sounds like a free ride on a famous name—was it really?

m039.text: Not at all! The name actually blocked its push into luxury Western markets.

m040.text: Postwar Japanese pencils seemed cheap, and foreigners just thought of ships!

m041.text: Would you coast on mistaken identity, or build a brand from scratch?

m042.text: In 1958, it launched premium pencil uni—meaning truly one of a kind!

m043.text: To stand out from Western yellow and green barrels, it tested 160 colors.

m044.text: It chose brownish wine-red with black-and-gold rings: the signature uni hue!

m045.text: And more: while rivals used paper boxes, it built a hinged plastic case!

m046.text: With ultra-smooth lead, hand-packing couldn't keep up—instant prestige.

m047.text: In 1966 came Hi-uni, spanning 22 grades from soft 10B to hard 10H.

m048.text: Who buys extremes like that? Even piano tuners snapped them up!

m049.text: The company confirmed: softest graphite lubricates piano key sides.

m050.text: And architects used the hardest grade to mark straight onto bricks!

m051.text: After shedding the zaibatsu shadow with uni, by the year 2000,

m052.text: ballpoints and mechanical pencils ruled daily writing. How to break out?

m053.text: Two 100-million-seller patented pens built the war chest to buy LAMY!

m054.text: Remember old oil-based pens? Clumpy ink that smeared at a touch.

m055.text: Water-based ink dried too slowly—then in 2006, Mitsubishi Pencil broke the deadlock.

m056.text: It launched low-viscosity oil ballpoint JETSTREAM, slashing writing drag!

m057.text: Ultra-smooth, fast-drying, rich black—selling over 100 million a year worldwide!

m058.text: Two years later, it brought that same obsession to mechanical pencils.

m059.text: Ever hate how mechanical pencil lead wears flat, thickens, and snaps?

m060.text: For decades, writers just kept rotating the pencil by hand.

m061.text: Its engineers refused to settle: if hands won't turn it, the lead will!

m062.text: In 2008, KURUTOGA arrived with micro-gears packed inside the tip.

m063.text: Every time you lift the pen, writing pressure turns the lead slightly.

m064.text: The tip stays razor-sharp and conical—clean lines, zero smudges!

m065.text: Over 100 million sold—Japan's number one mechanical pencil for 17 years straight!

m066.text: Beyond engineering, it even locked down its iconic color scheme:

m067.text: In 2018, uni's wine-red, black, and gold won a rare color trademark!

m068.text: Armed with patents and color rights, what wall did executives still hit?

m069.text: A tough reality: great at affordable tech, yet reliant on overseas distributors.

m070.text: Too distant from European taste, it missed mid-to-high-end fountain pens.

m071.text: Backed by a deep war chest, how would this independent firm flip the script?

m072.text: Just as everyone expected a slow grind, 2024 brought a shockwave!

m073.text: It announced a full buyout of Heidelberg fountain pen legend LAMY!

m074.text: From zero shares before, it bought 100% ownership in one bold sweep!

m075.text: Founded in 1930, LAMY is famed for Bauhaus functional design.

m076.text: 2023 revenue neared €77 million, with €5.9 million in operating profit.

m077.text: Launched in 1980, the safari pairs a triangular grip with a bold clip,

m078.text: gripping even thick denim pockets—a global icon for over 40 years!

m079.text: Once mistaken for a subsidiary, this pen maker bought a German design icon!

m080.text: You're probably wondering how a value Japanese firm complements German luxury.

m081.text: Line the two companies up side by side, and it's a match made in heaven.

m082.text: Almost zero overlap: Japan brings refills; Germany brings design and retail.

m083.text: It also gained metal fountain-nib craftsmanship, completing the puzzle.

m084.text: Cross-border deals often stumble—could this duo actually ship hits?

m085.text: Execution was blazing fast! By January next year, the first fusion hit shelves.

m086.text: LAMY safari JETSTREAM inside packed ultra-smooth ink into a German barrel!

m087.text: Best of all for fans, its M17 refill even fits older LAMY pens.

m088.text: At ¥3,630 per pen and ¥1,100 per refill, it became an instant hit!

m089.text: In March 2026, wave two arrived: a self-rotating mechanical pencil!

m090.text: LAMY safari KURUTOGA inside brought Japan's lead engine to the West.

m091.text: It redesigned a seamless German barrel housing a low-wobble engine.

m092.text: Priced at ¥4,180, it fused two design worlds into one!

m093.text: Forget hype—let's check the latest FY2025 consolidated earnings!

m094.text: Guess how big this former waterwheel shop has grown today?

m095.text: Annual revenue hit ¥89.8 billion, with operating margins above 10%.

m096.text: Even better: overseas sales reached ¥51.4 billion—over 57% of total!

m097.text: Europe alone topped ¥17.1 billion, becoming its biggest growth engine.

m098.text: Tangible fixed assets in Germany hit ¥7.8 billion—second only to Japan!

m099.text: European destocking and costs trimmed operating profit by 20%,

m100.text: yet its equity ratio sits at 75%, with filings stating: no parent company.

m101.text: The story isn't over: it's expanding supply chains across Asia and the West,

m102.text: targeting a record ¥94 billion in revenue for its 140th anniversary!

m103.text: Remember that misconception 90% of people got wrong at the start?

m104.text: People think it rode a conglomerate's coattails—the truth is the exact opposite.

m105.text: A century-old coincidence gave it a famous name, not global respect.

m106.text: Shedding that halo and obsessing over engineering won it the world stage!

m107.text: What turns an old workshop into a global giant isn't who you share a name with.

m108.text: It's generation after generation perfecting one tiny pen tip.

m109.text: Tell me in the comments: are you team JETSTREAM or team KURUTOGA?
